config.title: Memory Leak Hunt

intro.title: Memory Leak Hunt
intro.body: In this lesson, you will build a simple React component that demonstrates and fixes a common memory leak. You will learn how memory leaks occur when event listeners or subscriptions are not properly cleaned up in a component. The core concept involves using the useEffect hook to manage side effects and ensure cleanup when the component unmounts. You will work with TypeScript for type safety and React's lifecycle methods to prevent resource waste. By the end, you'll understand how to identify and resolve memory leaks in your React applications.
intro.usecase: Memory leak prevention is critical in long-running React applications like data dashboards, real-time monitoring tools, and complex admin panels. Developers encounter leaks when components with subscriptions, timers, or event listeners unmount without cleanup—causing performance degradation and crashes over time. For example, a financial dashboard with live charts must properly clean up WebSocket connections and interval timers when users switch views. Similarly, e-commerce filters with dynamic data fetching need to cancel pending requests when components are removed to prevent memory bloat.

objectives: Implement a React component with a memory leak using setInterval
Apply the useEffect cleanup function to prevent memory leaks
Construct a TypeScript interface for component state with timer management
Configure event handlers to start and stop interval-based operations
Update component state safely within useEffect dependencies
Bind cleanup logic to component unmounting lifecycle
Control timer references using useRef to avoid stale closures

steps.title: Import React, useState, and useEffect
steps.instruction: Import React, useState, and useEffect from 'react'.
steps.hint: Write the import statement at the top of the file. Use destructuring to import all three from the 'react' package.
steps.analogousExample:
// Example: importing multiple hooks
import React, { useState, useEffect } from 'react';
steps.expectedOutcome: You will have the necessary imports to use React components, state management, and side effects in this lesson.
successCriteria: React, useState, and useEffect are imported from 'react'.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You imported some of the required items. Make sure to import React, useState, and useEffect from 'react'.
steps.feedbackWrong: The import statement is missing or incorrect. You need to import React, useState, and useEffect from 'react'.

steps.title: Create the main App component
steps.instruction: Create a functional component named App that returns a JSX element. The component should be defined using either a function declaration or arrow function syntax.
steps.hint: Start by writing 'function App()' or 'const App = () =>', then add curly braces and return a simple JSX element like a div.
steps.seedCode:
import React, { useState, useEffect } from 'react';

// Create the App component here
steps.expectedOutcome: The App component is defined and returns a JSX element.
successCriteria: App component is defined as a function that returns JSX.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure the App component returns a JSX element (like a div).
steps.feedbackWrong: The App component isn't properly defined. Remember to create a function named App that returns JSX.

steps.title: Initialize state for a counter
steps.instruction: Inside your App component, declare a state variable named 'count' with its setter 'setCount' using useState, initialized to 0.
steps.hint: Use useState<number>(0) to create a number state with TypeScript.
steps.analogousExample:
// Example: initializing a number state
const [score, setScore] = useState<number>(0);
steps.expectedOutcome: The App component now has a count state variable initialized to 0, ready to track a counter value.
successCriteria: A state variable 'count' with setter 'setCount' is declared using useState, initialized to 0, with proper TypeScript typing.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close. Make sure you're using useState with <number> type and initializing to 0.
steps.feedbackWrong: The count state wasn't properly initialized. Check the useState syntax and TypeScript typing.

steps.title: Define a handler to start the timer
steps.instruction: Inside your App component, define a function named startTimer that sets up an interval to increment the count state every second and stores the interval ID in the timerId state.
steps.hint: Use setInterval to create a timer that runs every 1000 milliseconds. Inside the interval callback, update the count state using its setter function. Store the interval ID returned by setInterval in the timerId state.
steps.expectedOutcome: A startTimer function is defined in the component that sets an interval to update count and stores the interval ID.
successCriteria: The startTimer function is defined, uses setInterval with a 1000ms delay, increments count inside the interval callback, and stores the interval ID in timerId state.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You've defined a function, but make sure it: 1) uses setInterval with 1000ms, 2) increments count inside the callback, and 3) stores the interval ID in timerId state.
steps.feedbackWrong: The startTimer function isn't defined correctly. It should create an interval that updates count every second and saves the interval ID to timerId.

steps.title: Define stopTimer and add a useEffect cleanup demo
steps.instruction: Inside your App component, define a function named stopTimer that clears the running interval using clearInterval with the current timerId (and resets timerId if you clear it). After that, add a useEffect hook that logs 'Timer started' to the console when the component mounts, and returns a cleanup function that logs 'Timer cleaned up'.
steps.hint: Place the useEffect inside the component body, after your state declarations and handler functions. Use an empty dependency array [] to run only on mount.
steps.expectedOutcome: The useEffect hook is added with proper logging and a cleanup function, demonstrating how to prevent memory leaks by cleaning up side effects.
successCriteria: A useEffect hook is present with console.log('Timer started'), an empty dependency array [], and returns a cleanup function that logs 'Timer cleaned up'.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but check that your useEffect has both the initial log and returns a cleanup function with the correct log messages.
steps.feedbackWrong: The useEffect hook is missing or incomplete. Remember to include both the effect body and the cleanup function with the specified log messages.

steps.title: Add the counter display and timer control buttons
steps.instruction: Inside your component's return statement, add a paragraph element that displays the current count value and two buttons: one labeled 'Start Timer' that calls startTimer when clicked, and one labeled 'Stop Timer' that calls stopTimer when clicked.
steps.hint:
Use JSX syntax:

{count}

for the display and for the first button.
steps.expectedOutcome: The UI will show the current count value and two interactive buttons to control the timer.
successCriteria: The return statement contains a paragraph displaying the count value and two buttons with correct labels and onClick handlers wired to startTimer and stopTimer.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure you have all three elements: the paragraph showing count, and both buttons with correct labels and onClick handlers.
steps.feedbackWrong: The UI elements aren't properly implemented. Check that you're displaying the count value and both buttons have the correct onClick handlers.

steps.title: Add instructions and warnings about memory leaks
steps.instruction: Add a paragraph below the existing buttons that explains what memory leaks are and why cleanup is important.
steps.hint:

element with educational text about memory leaks and the cleanup function in useEffect.

steps.expectedOutcome: The UI now includes educational text explaining memory leaks and cleanup importance.
successCriteria: A paragraph element with text about memory leaks and cleanup is added to the JSX.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You added some text, but make sure it clearly explains what memory leaks are and why cleanup is necessary.
steps.feedbackWrong:
The paragraph about memory leaks wasn't added. Add a

element with explanatory text below the buttons.
